topic: Clean Air Act, Montreal Protocol and Section 608 rules

notes.front: What is the EPA, and what do its Section 608 regulations require of technicians?
notes.back: The United States Environmental Protection Agency. Its regulations require technicians whose work could release refrigerants into the atmosphere to be certified.
notes.explanation: The rules are EPA regulations made under the Clean Air Act, setting who must be certified and for which equipment.
notes.example: Like a national licensing authority: it does not run the tests itself, but it approves the organisations that do.
notes.evidence: EPA regulations (40 CFR Part 82, Subpart F) under Section 608 of the Clean Air Act require that technicians who maintain, service, repair, or dispose of equipment that could release refrigerants into the atmosphere must be certified.
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Requirements, “Requirements”

notes.front: What is the Clean Air Act (CAA), and what does its Title VI do?
notes.back: A United States law, amended by Congress in 1990. Its Title VI directs the EPA to protect the ozone layer.
notes.explanation: Title VI works through regulatory and voluntary programmes; its sections cover ODS production, recycling and handling of ODS, evaluation of substitutes and public education.
notes.example: Like a national rulebook with chapters: Title VI is the chapter on protecting the ozone layer.
notes.evidence: A law amended by Congress in 1990. Title VI of the CAA directs EPA to protect the ozone layer through several regulatory and voluntary programs. Sections within Title VI cover production of ozone-depleting substances (ODS), the recycling and handling of ODS, the evaluation of substitutes, and efforts to educate the public.
notes.source: US EPA, Phaseout of Class II Ozone-Depleting Substances, glossary entry “Clean Air Act”

notes.front: What does Section 608 of the Clean Air Act require, as applied by the EPA's regulations?
notes.back: That technicians who maintain, service, repair or dispose of equipment that could release refrigerants into the atmosphere are certified.
notes.explanation: The duty follows the work, not the job title: anyone doing work that could let refrigerant escape to the atmosphere is covered.
notes.example: Like a driving licence for refrigerant work: whoever connects gauges to a chiller needs one, whatever their job title.
notes.evidence: EPA regulations (40 CFR Part 82, Subpart F) under Section 608 of the Clean Air Act require that technicians who maintain, service, repair, or dispose of equipment that could release refrigerants into the atmosphere must be certified.
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Requirements, “Requirements”

notes.front: What is the Montreal Protocol?
notes.back: The international treaty governing the protection of stratospheric ozone. With its amendments, it controls the phaseout of ODS production and use.
notes.explanation: Its full name is the Montreal Protocol on Substances That Deplete the Ozone Layer, and the United States phaseout schedule is set to meet it.
notes.example: Like a global timetable for switching off supply: the Parties agree when production of each group of chemicals must end.
notes.evidence: The international treaty governing the protection of stratospheric ozone. The Montreal Protocol on Substances That Deplete the Ozone Layer and its amendments control the phaseout of ODS production and use.
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, Core, “Clean Air Act and Montreal Protocol” (glossary entry “Montreal Protocol”)

notes.front: What is a de minimis release?
notes.back: A release of refrigerant that happens during good faith attempts to recycle or recover refrigerants. It is not subject to the venting prohibition.
notes.explanation: The allowance is conditional: except for exempt substitutes, a release is de minimis only when the listed practices and requirements are being followed.
notes.example: Like crumbs dropped while carefully carrying a cake: a small loss during an honest, rule-following attempt, not a dumped cake.
notes.evidence: De minimis releases associated with good faith attempts to recycle or recover refrigerants are not subject to this prohibition. Except for exempt substitutes, refrigerant releases are de minimis only if they occur when:
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What is an exempt substitute?
notes.back: A substitute, used in an end-use listed in 82.154(a)(1), that is exempt from the venting prohibition and from the rest of Subpart F.
notes.explanation: Exemption depends on the chemical and the end-use together. Every other substitute and end-use is a non-exempt substitute.
notes.example: Like a permit valid only on certain streets: the same gas can be exempt in one kind of appliance and not in another.
notes.evidence: the term "exempt substitutes" refers to certain substitutes when used in certain end-uses that are specified in § 82.154(a)(1) as exempt from the venting prohibition and the requirements of this subpart, and the term "non-exempt substitutes" refers to all other substitutes and end-uses not so specified in § 82.154(a)(1).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Under Subpart F, what is an appliance?
notes.back: Any household or commercial device that contains and uses a class I or class II substance, or a substitute, as a refrigerant.
notes.explanation: The definition names air conditioners, motor vehicle air conditioners, refrigerators, chillers and freezers, and counts each independent circuit of a multi-circuit system separately.
notes.example: Like a household fridge or an office chiller: both hold and use refrigerant, so both are appliances.
notes.evidence: Appliance means any device which contains and uses a class I or class II substance or substitute as a refrigerant and which is used for household or commercial purposes, including any air conditioner, motor vehicle air conditioner, refrigerator, chiller, or freezer. For a system with multiple circuits, each independent circuit is considered a separate appliance.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What is a motor vehicle air conditioner (MVAC), and which certification covers paid MVAC service work?
notes.back: The air conditioner of a motor vehicle. People who service MVACs for consideration are certified under subpart B, not as Section 608 technicians.
notes.explanation: For buying MVAC refrigerant, the EPA's sales restriction page refers to this credential as Section 609 Technician Certification.
notes.example: Like the air conditioning in a delivery van, as opposed to the unit that cools the depot.
notes.evidence: Persons who maintain, service, or repair MVAC appliances for consideration must be certified in accordance with 40 CFR part 82, subpart B.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What is an MVAC-like appliance?
notes.back: An open-drive compressor air conditioner, with a full charge of 20 pounds or less, that cools the cab of an off-road vehicle or equipment.
notes.explanation: Air conditioning on agricultural or construction vehicles is the typical case the definition names.
notes.example: Like the cab air conditioning on a combine harvester working in a field, rather than on a car on the road.
notes.evidence: MVAC-like appliance means a mechanical vapor compression, open-drive compressor appliance with a full charge of 20 pounds or less of refrigerant used to cool the driver's or passenger's compartment of off-road vehicles or equipment. This includes, but is not limited to, the air-conditioning equipment found on agricultural or construction vehicles.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What is a very high-pressure appliance?
notes.back: One whose refrigerant has a critical temperature below 104 °F, or a liquid phase saturation pressure above 355 psia at 104 °F.
notes.explanation: The class is set by the refrigerant's properties at 104 °F, not by the size of the appliance.
notes.example: Like a low-temperature system charged with R-508B, one of the examples the definition gives.
notes.evidence: Very high-pressure appliance means an appliance that uses a refrigerant with a critical temperature below 104 °F or with a liquid phase saturation pressure above 355 psia at 104 °F. Examples include but are not limited to appliances using R-13, R-23, R-503, R-508A, and R-508B.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What is a high-pressure appliance?
notes.back: One whose refrigerant has a liquid phase saturation pressure between 170 psia and 355 psia at 104 °F.
notes.explanation: Each pressure class is a band of saturation pressure at 104 °F; this band sits above the medium class and below the very high class.
notes.example: Like a packaged unit charged with R-407C, one of the examples the definition lists.
notes.evidence: High-pressure appliance means an appliance that uses a refrigerant with a liquid phase saturation pressure between 170 psia and 355 psia at 104 °F. Examples include but are not limited to appliances using R-22, R-407A, R-407C, R-410A, and R-502.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What is a medium-pressure appliance?
notes.back: One whose refrigerant has a liquid phase saturation pressure between 45 psia and 170 psia at 104 °F.
notes.explanation: It is the band between the low-pressure class (below 45 psia) and the high-pressure class (from 170 psia).
notes.example: Like a system charged with R-124, one of the examples the definition lists.
notes.evidence: Medium-pressure appliance means an appliance that uses a refrigerant with a liquid phase saturation pressure between 45 psia and 170 psia at 104 °F. Examples include but are not limited to appliances using R-114, R-124, R-12, R-134a, and R-500.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What is a low-pressure appliance?
notes.back: One whose refrigerant has a liquid phase saturation pressure below 45 psia at 104 °F.
notes.explanation: It is the lowest of the four pressure bands, all measured at the same reference temperature of 104 °F.
notes.example: Like a large chiller charged with R-245fa, one of the examples the definition lists.
notes.evidence: Low-pressure appliance means an appliance that uses a refrigerant with a liquid phase saturation pressure below 45 psia at 104 °F. Examples include but are not limited to appliances using R-11, R-123, R-113, and R-245fa.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What is self-contained recovery equipment?
notes.back: Recovery or recycling equipment that can remove refrigerant from an appliance without help from components contained in the appliance.
notes.explanation: Everything needed to move the refrigerant is in the equipment itself, so the appliance's own parts need not be working.
notes.example: Like a portable pump that empties a tank on its own power, needing nothing from the tank.
notes.evidence: Self-contained recovery equipment means refrigerant recovery and/or recycling equipment that is capable of removing the refrigerant from an appliance without the assistance of components contained in the appliance.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What is system-dependent recovery equipment?
notes.back: Recovery equipment that needs the assistance of components contained in an appliance to remove the refrigerant from it.
notes.explanation: It cannot do the job alone: parts inside the appliance being emptied have to help move the refrigerant out.
notes.example: Like siphoning fuel with help from the tank's own pressure: it only works with help from the system being emptied.
notes.evidence: System-dependent recovery equipment means refrigerant recovery equipment that requires the assistance of components contained in an appliance to remove the refrigerant from the appliance.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What role does the Air-Conditioning, Heating, and Refrigeration Institute (AHRI) have under the Section 608 rules?
notes.back: It is one of the two organisations the EPA has approved to certify refrigerant recycling and recovery equipment.
notes.explanation: Both approved organisations can provide information on the equipment they have certified.
notes.example: Like a testing house whose stamp tells a buyer that a recovery machine meets the federal minimum standards.
notes.evidence: EPA has approved the Air-Conditioning, Heating, and Refrigeration Institute (AHRI) and Underwriters Laboratories (UL)to certify recycling and recovery equipment. Both organizations can provide information on certified equipment.
notes.source: US EPA, Refrigerant Recovery and Recycling Equipment Certification, “EPA-Approved Testing Organizations”

notes.front: What is AHRI Standard 700-2016 used for in the Section 608 rules?
notes.back: It is the basis of the purity level in Appendix A to Subpart F, which used refrigerant must reach to count as reclaimed.
notes.explanation: Meeting the purity level is not enough on paper: it must be verified with the laboratory protocol set out in the same standard.
notes.example: Like a food-grade specification: recovered refrigerant has to be cleaned up to it, and tested, before it counts as reclaimed.
notes.evidence: To be properly reclaimed, used refrigerant must be reprocessed to at least the purity level specified in Appendix A to 40 CFR Part 82, Subpart F [based on Air Conditioning, Heating, and Refrigeration Institute (AHRI) Standard 700-2016]. This purity level must be verified using the laboratory protocol set forth in this same standard.
notes.source: US EPA, Stationary Refrigeration Refrigerant Reclamation Requirements, “Refrigerant Reclamation Requirements”

notes.front: What is the refrigerant sales restriction?
notes.back: The rule that only EPA-certified technicians may buy ODS or non-ozone-depleting substitutes used as refrigerants, with limited exceptions.
notes.explanation: Buyers may also only purchase refrigerant that fits the appliances their own certification covers.
notes.example: Like prescription-only medicine: the counter staff must see proof of certification before handing over a cylinder.
notes.evidence: Only EPA-certified technicians are allowed to purchase ozone-depleting substances (ODS) or non-ozone depleting substitutes used as refrigerants, with limited exceptions. Refrigerant can only be sold to technicians certified under the Section 608 or Section 609 technician certification programs, where individuals may only purchase refrigerant consistent with the appliances covered by their certification.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What is a self-sealing valve?
notes.back: A valve on a refrigerant container that seals automatically when not dispensing, and meets the performance criteria in 82.154(c)(2).
notes.explanation: It is defined by behaviour and by a tested standard, not just by the valve's design.
notes.example: Like the valve on a squeezy drinks bottle that closes itself as soon as you stop pressing.
notes.evidence: Self-sealing valve means a valve affixed to a container of refrigerant that automatically seals when not dispensing refrigerant and meets or exceeds established performance criteria as identified in § 82.154(c)(2).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Under Subpart F, who is a technician?
notes.back: Anyone who, while maintaining, servicing or repairing an appliance other than an MVAC, could reasonably be expected to violate the integrity of the refrigerant circuit.
notes.explanation: The test is the risk of release: violating the circuit's integrity is what could let refrigerant escape into the environment.
notes.example: Like a building owner who opens their own rooftop unit's refrigerant circuit to fix it: still a technician under the rules.
notes.evidence: Technician means any person who in the course of maintenance, service, or repair of an appliance (except MVACs) could be reasonably expected to violate the integrity of the refrigerant circuit and therefore release refrigerants into the environment.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Under Subpart F, who is an apprentice?
notes.back: A person currently registered as an apprentice in appliance work with the Department of Labor's Office of Apprenticeship, or a state council it recognises.
notes.explanation: It is a registered status with a set time limit, not simply being new to the trade.
notes.example: Like a registered electrician's apprentice on a formal scheme, not a helper picked up for a busy summer.
notes.evidence: Apprentice means any person who is currently registered as an apprentice in maintenance, service, repair, or disposal of appliances with the U.S. Department of Labor's Office of Apprenticeship (or a State Apprenticeship Council recognized by the Office of Apprenticeship). A person may only be an apprentice for two years from the date of first registering with that office.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What does Type I certification cover?
notes.back: Maintaining, servicing or repairing small appliances.
notes.explanation: Small appliances are the factory-sealed units holding five pounds or less of refrigerant, such as household refrigerators and room air conditioners.
notes.example: Like the certificate a technician needs to repair a dehumidifier or a drinking water cooler.
notes.evidence: Persons who maintain, service, or repair small appliances must be certified as Type I technicians.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What does Type II certification cover?
notes.back: Maintaining, servicing, repairing or disposing of medium-, high- and very high-pressure appliances, other than small appliances, MVACs and MVAC-like appliances.
notes.explanation: Note the medium-pressure class: the rule puts it under Type II even though some summaries mention only high and very high pressure.
notes.example: Like the certificate needed to service a supermarket display case running on R-407A.
notes.evidence: Persons who maintain, service, repair, or dispose of medium-, high-, or very high-pressure appliances (except small appliances, MVACs, and MVAC-like appliances) must be certified as Type II technicians.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What does Type III certification cover?
notes.back: Maintaining, servicing, repairing or disposing of low-pressure appliances.
notes.explanation: Low-pressure appliances use refrigerants with a saturation pressure below 45 psia at 104 °F, so they form their own certification type.
notes.example: Like the certificate needed to work on a large building chiller charged with R-113.
notes.evidence: Persons who maintain, service, repair, or dispose of low-pressure appliances must be certified as Type III technicians.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What does Universal certification cover?
notes.back: All the appliances covered by Types I, II and III together.
notes.explanation: It is for technicians whose work crosses the categories, from small appliances to low-pressure chillers.
notes.example: Like an all-classes driving licence: one credential for every vehicle category.
notes.evidence: Persons who maintain, service, repair, or dispose of all appliances described in paragraph (a)(1)(i) through (iii) of this section must be certified as Universal technicians.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Who is the final processor in the disposal of a small appliance, MVAC or MVAC-like appliance?
notes.back: The person who takes the final step in the disposal process, such as a scrap recycler or landfill operator.
notes.explanation: The list of examples is open: scrap recyclers and landfill operators are named, but not as the only ones.
notes.example: Like the scrapyard that finally shreds an old chest freezer after it has passed through other hands.
notes.evidence: The final processor—i.e., persons who take the final step in the disposal process (including but not limited to scrap recyclers and landfill operators) of a small appliance, MVAC, or MVAC-like appliance—must either:
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What is a process stub?
notes.back: Tubing giving access to the refrigerant inside a small appliance or room air conditioner, which can be resealed after repair or service.
notes.explanation: It provides a way in to the refrigerant that can be closed off again once the work is done.
notes.example: Like the resealable spout on a sealed carton: a way in that can be shut again afterwards.
notes.evidence: Process stub means a length of tubing that provides access to the refrigerant inside a small appliance or room air conditioner and that can be resealed at the conclusion of repair or service.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What is the EPA's Significant New Alternatives Policy (SNAP) programme?
notes.back: The programme through which the EPA evaluates alternatives to HCFCs and other ozone-depleting substances.
notes.explanation: It runs alongside the phaseout, which restricts the use of the HCFCs being replaced.
notes.example: Like an approvals list for replacement parts: only alternatives found acceptable make it on.
notes.evidence: The phaseout restricts the use of these HCFCs, and EPA continues to evaluate HCFC alternatives through its Significant New Alternatives Policy (SNAP) program.
notes.source: US EPA, Phaseout of Class II Ozone-Depleting Substances, “Common HCFCs and Their Uses”

notes.front: What are three of the four areas that sections of Clean Air Act Title VI cover?
notes.back: Production of ODS, recycling and handling of ODS, and evaluation of substitutes.
notes.explanation: The fourth area is efforts to educate the public; together they make up the ozone programmes the EPA runs under Title VI.
notes.evidence: Sections within Title VI cover production of ozone-depleting substances (ODS), the recycling and handling of ODS, the evaluation of substitutes, and efforts to educate the public.
notes.source: US EPA, Phaseout of Class II Ozone-Depleting Substances, glossary entry “Clean Air Act”

notes.front: A town runs a campaign teaching residents how the ozone layer is protected. Which Title VI area does that match?
notes.back: Efforts to educate the public.
notes.explanation: Title VI is not only about regulation: its sections also cover education, alongside production limits, recycling and handling, and substitutes.
notes.evidence: Sections within Title VI cover production of ozone-depleting substances (ODS), the recycling and handling of ODS, the evaluation of substitutes, and efforts to educate the public.
notes.source: US EPA, Phaseout of Class II Ozone-Depleting Substances, glossary entry “Clean Air Act”

notes.front: CFCs are gases covered under the {{c1::1987}} Montreal Protocol.
notes.explanation: The same entry notes they drift into the upper atmosphere, not being destroyed lower down, and break down ozone there.
notes.evidence: Gases covered under the 1987 Montreal Protocol and used for refrigeration, air conditioning, packaging, insulation, solvents, or aerosol propellants. Since they are not destroyed in the lower atmosphere, CFCs drift into the upper atmosphere
notes.source: US EPA, Basic Ozone Layer Science, “II. Ozone Depletion” (glossary entry “chlorofluorocarbons”)

notes.front: As a Party to the Montreal Protocol, by when must the United States complete its HCFC phaseout?
notes.explanation: The cut is incremental: HCFC use had to be at least 90 percent below baseline in 2015 and 99.5 percent below in 2020.
notes.evidence: the United States must incrementally decrease HCFC consumption and production, culminating in a complete HCFC phaseout in 2030. HCFC usage must be reduced to at least 90 percent below baseline levels in 2015 and to at least 99.5 percent below baseline levels in 2020.
notes.source: US EPA, Phaseout of Class II Ozone-Depleting Substances, “The Phaseout of HCFCs”

notes.front: A customer asks why new R-22 has become scarce when their old air conditioner is still legal to run. Which international agreement is the United States schedule built to meet?
notes.back: The Montreal Protocol.
notes.explanation: The United States phaseout of HCFCs, including HCFC-22, is set out as its schedule for meeting the Montreal Protocol's requirements.
notes.evidence: The U.S. schedule for meeting the Montreal Protocol phaseout requirements is summarized in the following table.
notes.source: US EPA, Phaseout of Class II Ozone-Depleting Substances, “The Phaseout of HCFCs”

notes.front: When did the ban on producing and importing class I ODS, other than halons and methyl bromide, take effect?
notes.back: 1 January 1996.
notes.explanation: Halons went two years earlier, on 1 January 1994, and the source notes several exemptions from the phaseout.
notes.evidence: The ban on production and import of halons took effect on January 1, 1994. The ban on production and import of other Class I ODS—excluding methyl bromide—took effect on January 1, 1996. There are several exemptions from the phaseout.
notes.source: US EPA, Phaseout of Class I Ozone-Depleting Substances, introduction

notes.front: A customer asks whether newly made CFC-12 can still be produced or imported in the United States for their old unit. Which date answers this?
notes.back: 1 January 1996, when the ban on producing and importing class I ODS (other than methyl bromide) took effect.
notes.explanation: CFC-12 is a class I ODS and not methyl bromide, so the 1996 ban covers it, subject to the exemptions the source mentions.
notes.evidence: The ban on production and import of other Class I ODS—excluding methyl bromide—took effect on January 1, 1996. There are several exemptions from the phaseout.
notes.source: US EPA, Phaseout of Class I Ozone-Depleting Substances, introduction

notes.front: From 2010, what restriction applied to producing and importing HCFC-22?
notes.back: No production or import except for use in equipment manufactured before 1 January 2010.
notes.explanation: Existing equipment could still be supplied, but equipment made from 2010 could not rely on newly produced HCFC-22.
notes.evidence: No production or import of HCFC-142b and HCFC-22, except for use in equipment manufactured before January 1, 2010
notes.source: US EPA, Phaseout of Class II Ozone-Depleting Substances, “The Phaseout of HCFCs”

notes.front: What has the rule been on producing and importing HCFC-22 since 2020?
notes.back: No production or import of HCFC-22 or HCFC-142b.
notes.explanation: The 2020 step went with a 99.5 percent reduction in HCFC consumption and production from baseline.
notes.evidence: No production or import of HCFC-142b and HCFC-22 | 2020 | 99.5%
notes.source: US EPA, Phaseout of Class II Ozone-Depleting Substances, “The Phaseout of HCFCs”

notes.front: Since the 2020 production ban, can existing HCFC-22 equipment still be serviced with R-22?
notes.back: Yes. HCFC-22 can be used to service existing equipment, and servicing includes replacing failed components.
notes.explanation: The phaseout ends production and import; it does not stop the use of HCFC-22 already available for existing equipment.
notes.evidence: Yes, HCFC-22 (also called R-22) can be used to service existing equipment. Servicing includes replacing failed components.
notes.source: US EPA, Technicians and Contractors: Frequent Questions, “Can existing equipment containing HCFC-22 still be serviced?”

notes.front: A homeowner's R-22 air conditioner works well, but a salesperson says the law now forces them to replace it. Is that right?
notes.back: No. Continued use of existing HCFC-22 appliances is not banned, and there is no EPA mandate to convert them.
notes.explanation: Phased out is not banned: what ended was new production and import, not the use of equipment already installed.
notes.evidence: the continued use of existing appliances containing HCFC-22 is not banned and that there is no EPA mandate for converting existing HCFC-22 equipment.
notes.source: US EPA, Technicians and Contractors: Frequent Questions, “Should I discuss the HCFC phaseout with my customers?”

notes.front: What does the venting prohibition in 82.154(a) forbid?
notes.back: Anyone maintaining, servicing, repairing or disposing of an appliance knowingly venting or otherwise releasing its refrigerant into the environment.
notes.explanation: The key word is “knowingly”: the rule targets deliberate releases made in the course of that work.
notes.evidence: No person maintaining, servicing, repairing, or disposing of an appliance or industrial process refrigeration may knowingly vent or otherwise release into the environment any refrigerant from such appliances.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: To save time, a technician opens a valve and lets a system's refrigerant blow off before replacing a component. Which rule has been broken?
notes.back: The venting prohibition: knowingly releasing refrigerant while servicing an appliance.
notes.explanation: Replacing a component is servicing, and the release was deliberate, so both elements of the prohibition are met.
notes.evidence: No person maintaining, servicing, repairing, or disposing of an appliance or industrial process refrigeration may knowingly vent or otherwise release into the environment any refrigerant from such appliances.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: No person maintaining, servicing, repairing or {{c1::disposing of}} an appliance may knowingly vent any refrigerant from it.
notes.explanation: Disposal is named alongside servicing, so the end of an appliance's life is no exception.
notes.evidence: No person maintaining, servicing, repairing, or disposing of an appliance or industrial process refrigeration may knowingly vent or otherwise release into the environment any refrigerant from such appliances.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A demolition crew cuts the refrigerant lines of an old rooftop unit so they can haul it away, releasing the charge. Does the venting prohibition apply?
notes.back: Yes. It applies to anyone disposing of an appliance, not only to those servicing it.
notes.explanation: Cutting the lines knowingly releases the refrigerant during disposal, which the prohibition covers.
notes.evidence: No person maintaining, servicing, repairing, or disposing of an appliance or industrial process refrigeration may knowingly vent or otherwise release into the environment any refrigerant from such appliances.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Knowingly releasing a class I, class II or non-exempt substitute refrigerant {{c1::after its recovery}} from an appliance also violates the venting prohibition.
notes.explanation: Getting refrigerant into a recovery cylinder does not make it free to release later.
notes.evidence: The knowing release of a class I or class II refrigerant or a non-exempt substitute refrigerant after its recovery from an appliance is a violation of the venting prohibition.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Is it legal to knowingly vent HFC refrigerants?
notes.back: No. It is illegal, just as it is for ozone-depleting refrigerants like HCFC-22.
notes.explanation: The same answer adds that only specific HFCs are acceptable substitutes for each end use, on a list the SNAP programme maintains.
notes.evidence: Yes, only specific HFC refrigerants are acceptable substitutes for different end uses. EPA's SNAP program maintains a list of acceptable refrigerant substitutes. It is also illegal to knowingly vent or release these refrigerants— just as it is for ozone-depleting refrigerants like HCFC-22.
notes.source: US EPA, Technicians and Contractors: Frequent Questions, “Are there any limitations on the use of HFC refrigerants?”

notes.front: A technician says it is fine to vent an HFC system because HFCs do not harm the ozone layer. How does the 2020 rule change answer this?
notes.back: It does not help: the 2020 rule left the prohibition on knowingly releasing non-ozone-depleting refrigerants, including HFCs, in place.
notes.explanation: Zero ozone depletion does not take a refrigerant outside the venting prohibition.
notes.evidence: does not affect the Clean Air Act prohibition on intentionally venting or otherwise knowingly releasing ozone-depleting and non-ozone depleting refrigerant (including HFCs) into the environment.
notes.source: US EPA, Regulatory Updates: Section 608 Refrigerant Management Regulations, “2020 Rule Summary”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A little refrigerant escapes as a technician disconnects a hose after charging an appliance, while following the rules. Is that a violation?
notes.back: No. It is a de minimis release made during good faith attempts to recapture, recycle or safely dispose of refrigerant.
notes.explanation: The venting page names releases when connecting or disconnecting hoses as part of the de minimis allowance.
notes.evidence: quantities of refrigerant released while making good faith attempts to recapture and recycle or safely dispose of refrigerant including releases that occur when connecting or disconnecting hoses to charge or service appliances.
notes.source: US EPA, Stationary Refrigeration: Prohibition on Venting Refrigerants, “Types of Releases”

notes.front: Is refrigerant emitted through mechanical purging or leaks during normal operation covered by the venting prohibition?
notes.back: No. Emissions during normal operation are a permitted type of release, unlike those during maintenance, servicing, repair or disposal.
notes.explanation: Permitted is not ignored: large leaking equipment must still be repaired. Under Subpart F that means 50 lb or more of class I or II refrigerant; many HFC systems fall under a separate rule (section 84.106) from 2026.
notes.evidence: Refrigerant emitted during the normal operation of air-conditioning and refrigeration equipment (as opposed to during the maintenance, servicing, repair, or disposal of this equipment), such as from mechanical purging and leaks. However, EPA requires that leaks above a certain size be repaired in equipment that contains 50 pounds of refrigerant or more.
notes.source: US EPA, Stationary Refrigeration: Prohibition on Venting Refrigerants, “Types of Releases”

notes.front: Besides de minimis releases and normal-operation emissions, what is the third permitted type of release?
notes.back: Releases of substitute refrigerants that EPA has determined do not pose a threat to the environment.
notes.explanation: In the regulation these are the exempt substitutes, each exempt only in its listed end-uses.
notes.evidence: Releases of substitute refrigerants that EPA has determined do not pose a threat to the environment.
notes.source: US EPA, Stationary Refrigeration: Prohibition on Venting Refrigerants, “Types of Releases”

notes.front: Among the conditions for a release to be de minimis, what must be true of recovery equipment, certification and reclamation?
notes.back: Compliant recovery or recycling machines are used whenever refrigerant is removed, and the certification and reclamation requirements are observed.
notes.explanation: The practices in 82.155 and 82.156 must also be observed, and those in 82.157 for appliances containing class I or II refrigerant; good intentions alone do not make a release de minimis.
notes.evidence: recovery and/or recycling machines that meet the requirements in § 82.158 are used whenever refrigerant is removed from an appliance, the technician certification provisions in § 82.161 are observed, and the reclamation requirements in § 82.164 are observed
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A technician loses a little refrigerant while using a home-made recovery rig that meets no equipment standard. Is that loss de minimis?
notes.back: No. A release is de minimis only if recovery machines meeting the equipment requirements are used, among other conditions.
notes.explanation: The good faith allowance depends on following the rules, and using non-compliant recovery equipment breaks one of them.
notes.evidence: recovery and/or recycling machines that meet the requirements in § 82.158 are used whenever refrigerant is removed from an appliance, the technician certification provisions in § 82.161 are observed, and the reclamation requirements in § 82.164 are observed
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Besides the venting prohibition, what else are the listed substitutes in their listed end-uses exempt from?
notes.back: The other requirements of Subpart F.
notes.explanation: An exempt substitute sits outside the subpart's rules altogether, for example the invoice records sellers otherwise keep.
notes.evidence: the following substitutes in the following end-uses are exempt from this prohibition and from the requirements of this subpart:
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: In which end-uses is carbon dioxide exempt from the venting prohibition?
notes.back: In any application.
notes.explanation: Its exemption has no end-use limit, unlike most of the list.
notes.evidence: Carbon dioxide in any application;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: In which end-uses is nitrogen exempt from the venting prohibition?
notes.back: In any application.
notes.explanation: Like carbon dioxide and water, nitrogen is exempt without any end-use limit.
notes.evidence: Nitrogen in any application;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: In which end-uses is water exempt from the venting prohibition?
notes.back: In any application.
notes.explanation: Water is one of only three listed substances exempt in every application.
notes.evidence: Water in any application;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: In which end-uses is ammonia exempt from the venting prohibition?
notes.back: In commercial or industrial process refrigeration, or in absorption units.
notes.explanation: Outside those end-uses, ammonia is a non-exempt substitute.
notes.evidence: Ammonia in commercial or industrial process refrigeration or in absorption units;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: In which end-uses is chlorine exempt from the venting prohibition?
notes.back: In industrial process refrigeration used for processing chlorine and chlorine compounds.
notes.explanation: The exemption is tied to one industrial process, not to chlorine in general.
notes.evidence: Chlorine in industrial process refrigeration (processing of chlorine and chlorine compounds);
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: In which end-uses are hydrocarbons exempt from the venting prohibition?
notes.back: In industrial process refrigeration used for processing hydrocarbons.
notes.explanation: Other hydrocarbon uses are exempt only where a named hydrocarbon, such as propane, has its own listed end-uses.
notes.evidence: Hydrocarbons in industrial process refrigeration (processing of hydrocarbons);
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: In which end-uses is ethane (R-170) exempt from the venting prohibition?
notes.back: In very low temperature refrigeration equipment and equipment for non-mechanical heat transfer.
notes.explanation: Both listed end-uses are specialist, so ethane elsewhere is non-exempt.
notes.evidence: Ethane (R-170) in very low temperature refrigeration equipment and equipment for non-mechanical heat transfer;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: In which end-uses is propane (R-290) exempt from the venting prohibition?
notes.back: Among others: stand-alone retail food units, household refrigerators and freezers, and self-contained room air conditioners.
notes.explanation: The list also covers vending machines, commercial ice machines, very low temperature equipment and water coolers; food processing and dispensing equipment was added from 15 July 2024.
notes.evidence: Propane (R-290) in retail food refrigerators and freezers—stand-alone units; household refrigerators, freezers, and combination refrigerators and freezers; self-contained room air conditioners for residential and light commercial air-conditioning and heat pumps; vending machines; self-contained commercial ice machines, very low temperature refrigeration equipment, and water coolers; and effective July 15, 2024, retail food refrigeration—refrigerated food processing and dispensing equipment;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Propane in retail food refrigerated food processing and dispensing equipment is exempt from the venting prohibition effective {{c1::15 July 2024}}.
notes.explanation: It was the latest addition to propane's list of exempt end-uses, so older summaries leave it out.
notes.evidence: and effective July 15, 2024, retail food refrigeration—refrigerated food processing and dispensing equipment;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: In which end-uses is isobutane (R-600a) exempt from the venting prohibition?
notes.back: Stand-alone retail food refrigerators and freezers, household refrigerators and freezers, and vending machines.
notes.explanation: Its list is shorter than propane's: room air conditioners, for example, are not on it.
notes.evidence: Isobutane (R-600a) in retail food refrigerators and freezers (stand-alone units only); household refrigerators, freezers, and combination refrigerators and freezers; and vending machines;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: In which end-uses is R-441A exempt from the venting prohibition?
notes.back: Among others: stand-alone retail food units, household refrigerators and freezers, and self-contained room air conditioners.
notes.explanation: Its list also includes heat pumps and vending machines.
notes.evidence: R-441A in retail food refrigerators and freezers (stand-alone units only); household refrigerators, freezers, and combination refrigerators and freezers; self-contained room air conditioners for residential and light commercial air-conditioning; heat pumps; and vending machines.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A self-contained room air conditioner is charged with isobutane (R-600a). Is its isobutane an exempt substitute?
notes.back: No. Isobutane is exempt only in stand-alone retail food units, household refrigerators and freezers, and vending machines.
notes.explanation: Exemption goes by end-use, and room air conditioners are not on isobutane's list, so it is non-exempt there.
notes.evidence: Isobutane (R-600a) in retail food refrigerators and freezers (stand-alone units only); household refrigerators, freezers, and combination refrigerators and freezers; and vending machines;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: An office building's air-conditioning chiller (not an absorption unit) uses ammonia. Is the ammonia exempt from the venting prohibition?
notes.back: No. Ammonia is exempt only in commercial or industrial process refrigeration, or in absorption units.
notes.explanation: Office air conditioning is none of those end-uses, so the ammonia counts as a non-exempt substitute there.
notes.evidence: Ammonia in commercial or industrial process refrigeration or in absorption units;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Under Table 1 of the EPA’s penalty inflation rule, what is the maximum civil penalty under 42 U.S.C. 7413(b) for a Clean Air Act violation after 2 November 2015, assessed on or after 8 January 2025?
notes.back: $124,426 per day for each violation.
notes.explanation: The Act sets a daily maximum for each violation, and the EPA’s inflation rule raises it: for penalties assessed from 27 December 2023 until 8 January 2025 it was $121,275.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR 19.4 Table 1 as in force

notes.front: What was the civil penalty under 42 U.S.C. 7413(b) as originally enacted, before inflation adjustment?
notes.explanation: The Act set it at $25,000 per day for each violation; inflation adjustments have since raised it to $124,426, about five times as much.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR 19.4 Table 1 as in force

notes.front: An old study guide gives $37,500 as the Clean Air Act civil penalty. Is that the figure for a violation committed in 2026?
notes.back: No. For violations after 2 November 2015 assessed on or after 8 January 2025, Table 1 gives $124,426; $37,500 is an older Table 2 figure.
notes.explanation: Table 2 still governs older cases: $37,500 applies to violations after 6 December 2013 through 2 November 2015, which is why the old number still circulates.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR 19.4 Tables 1 and 2 as in force

notes.front: Which appliances does Subpart F apply to today?
notes.back: Appliances containing class I, class II or non-exempt substitute refrigerants, during maintenance, service, repair and disposal.
notes.explanation: The test outline still says CFCs or HCFCs; the current text adds non-exempt substitutes such as HFCs, and reaches disposal of small appliances and MVACs too.
notes.evidence: This subpart applies to any person maintaining, servicing, or repairing appliances containing class I, class II or non-exempt substitute refrigerants. This subpart also applies to persons disposing of such appliances (including small appliances and motor vehicle air conditioners)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Which equipment does the test outline leave out of the rule's coverage of air-conditioning and refrigeration equipment?
notes.back: Motor vehicle air conditioners.
notes.explanation: MVAC service work is certified separately, under subpart B, rather than under Section 608.
notes.evidence: all air-conditioning and refrigeration equipment containing CFCs or HCFCs except motor vehicle air conditioners
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, Core, “Section 608 Regulations”

notes.front: A contractor says he needs no Section 608 certification because he only works on HFC systems, and the test outline mentions only CFCs and HCFCs. Is he right?
notes.back: No. Since 1 January 2018, EPA certification has been required to service stationary systems containing HFCs.
notes.explanation: The outline predates the change; the current rules cover non-exempt substitutes such as HFCs.
notes.evidence: Yes, beginning January 1, 2018, EPA technician certification is required in order to service stationary refrigeration and air-conditioning systems containing HFCs.
notes.source: US EPA, Technicians and Contractors: Frequent Questions, “Is EPA technician certification required to service systems that use HFCs?”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A supermarket rack has three independent refrigerant circuits. How many appliances is that under the rules?
notes.back: Three: each independent circuit is a separate appliance.
notes.explanation: Counting by circuit matters because duties are applied appliance by appliance.
notes.evidence: For a system with multiple circuits, each independent circuit is considered a separate appliance.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Is Section 608 certification needed to pull the heel (the residue) out of an empty refrigerant cylinder?
notes.back: No. Cylinders that store or transport bulk refrigerant are not appliances.
notes.explanation: Certification attaches to work on appliances, and a bulk cylinder is not one.
notes.evidence: No. Cylinders that store or transport bulk refrigerant are not considered appliances.
notes.source: US EPA, Questions and Answers for Section 608 Certified Technicians, “General Questions”

notes.front: An off-road tractor's cab air conditioner runs on R-22. Is it an MVAC-like appliance?
notes.back: No. The MVAC-like definition is not intended to cover appliances using R-22.
notes.explanation: Cab size and vehicle type are not enough: the definition expressly leaves out R-22 appliances.
notes.evidence: This definition is not intended to cover appliances using R-22 refrigerant.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Which certification may a technician servicing MVAC-like appliances hold?
notes.back: Either Type II certification or certification under subpart B, the MVAC programme.
notes.explanation: MVAC-like appliances sit between the two programmes, so either credential is accepted for servicing them.
notes.evidence: Technicians who maintain, service, or repair MVAC-like appliances must either be certified as Type II technicians or be certified in accordance with 40 CFR part 82, subpart B.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A mechanic is paid to recharge a car's air conditioner. Does Section 608 Type II certification cover this work?
notes.back: No. Servicing MVACs for consideration requires certification under subpart B.
notes.explanation: A car's air conditioner is an MVAC, and paid MVAC work belongs to the MVAC programme, not Section 608.
notes.evidence: Persons who maintain, service, or repair MVAC appliances for consideration must be certified in accordance with 40 CFR part 82, subpart B.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: An appliance uses R-23. Which pressure class is it?
notes.back: Very high-pressure.
notes.explanation: R-23 is one of the definition's own examples for the very high class.
notes.evidence: Examples include but are not limited to appliances using R-13, R-23, R-503, R-508A, and R-508B.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: An appliance uses R-410A. Which pressure class is it?
notes.back: High-pressure.
notes.explanation: R-410A is listed as an example of the high class, alongside R-22.
notes.evidence: Examples include but are not limited to appliances using R-22, R-407A, R-407C, R-410A, and R-502.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: An appliance uses R-22. Which pressure class is it?
notes.back: High-pressure.
notes.explanation: R-22 heads the definition's list of high-pressure examples.
notes.evidence: Examples include but are not limited to appliances using R-22, R-407A, R-407C, R-410A, and R-502.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: An appliance uses R-134a. Which pressure class is it?
notes.back: Medium-pressure.
notes.explanation: Older summaries sort refrigerants into only high and low, but R-134a sits in the medium class.
notes.evidence: Examples include but are not limited to appliances using R-114, R-124, R-12, R-134a, and R-500.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: An appliance uses R-123. Which pressure class is it?
notes.back: Low-pressure.
notes.explanation: R-123 is one of the definition's own low-pressure examples.
notes.evidence: Examples include but are not limited to appliances using R-11, R-123, R-113, and R-245fa.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: The test outline speaks of high- and low-pressure refrigerants. How many appliance pressure classes does the current regulation define?
notes.back: Four. Medium-pressure and very high-pressure are the two classes the outline's wording leaves out.
notes.explanation: The medium class, from 45 to 170 psia at 104 °F, fills the gap between low and high.
notes.evidence: Medium-pressure appliance means an appliance that uses a refrigerant with a liquid phase saturation pressure between 45 psia and 170 psia at 104 °F.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Self-contained versus system-dependent recovery equipment: what separates them?
notes.back: Whether help from components inside the appliance is needed: system-dependent equipment needs it, self-contained equipment does not.
notes.explanation: That makes self-contained equipment independent of the state of the appliance's own parts.
notes.evidence: System-dependent recovery equipment means refrigerant recovery equipment that requires the assistance of components contained in an appliance to remove the refrigerant from the appliance.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A recovery device can only remove refrigerant with the help of components inside the appliance being serviced. Which type of recovery equipment is it?
notes.back: System-dependent recovery equipment.
notes.explanation: Relying on the appliance's own components is the defining feature of the system-dependent type.
notes.evidence: System-dependent recovery equipment means refrigerant recovery equipment that requires the assistance of components contained in an appliance to remove the refrigerant from the appliance.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A recovery machine removes refrigerant from an appliance whose own components give no help at all. Which type of recovery equipment is it?
notes.back: Self-contained recovery equipment.
notes.explanation: Working without the appliance's components is what the self-contained definition describes.
notes.evidence: Self-contained recovery equipment means refrigerant recovery and/or recycling equipment that is capable of removing the refrigerant from an appliance without the assistance of components contained in the appliance.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: When maintaining, servicing, repairing or disposing of an appliance, what must be true of the recovery or recycling equipment used?
notes.back: It must be certified for that type of refrigerant and appliance.
notes.explanation: The certification is specific: equipment certified for one kind of refrigerant or appliance does not cover every kind.
notes.evidence: Using recovery and/or recycling equipment that is certified for that type of refrigerant and appliance under § 82.158.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A technician builds a recovery rig from spare parts and uses it on an HFC system. Which requirement does this break?
notes.back: The requirement to use recovery equipment certified for that type of refrigerant and appliance.
notes.explanation: HFCs are non-exempt substitutes, so certified equipment is required for them just as for ODS.
notes.evidence: Using recovery and/or recycling equipment that is certified for that type of refrigerant and appliance under § 82.158.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Besides AHRI, which organisation has the EPA approved to certify recycling and recovery equipment?
notes.back: Underwriters Laboratories.
notes.explanation: Either approved organisation can provide information on the equipment it has certified.
notes.evidence: EPA has approved the Air-Conditioning, Heating, and Refrigeration Institute (AHRI) and Underwriters Laboratories (UL)to certify recycling and recovery equipment. Both organizations can provide information on certified equipment.
notes.source: US EPA, Refrigerant Recovery and Recycling Equipment Certification, “EPA-Approved Testing Organizations”

notes.front: How can certified recovery or recycling equipment be identified?
notes.back: By a label stating it has been certified to meet EPA's minimum requirements for recycling or recovery equipment for a stated category of appliance.
notes.explanation: The label names the appliance category, so it also shows what the equipment is certified for.
notes.evidence: to meet EPA's minimum requirements for recycling and/or recovery equipment intended for use with
notes.source: US EPA, Refrigerant Recovery and Recycling Equipment Certification, “EPA-Approved Testing Organizations”

notes.front: In the definition of certified recovery equipment, which date separates older equipment that only has to meet set standards from equipment certified by a testing organisation?
notes.back: 15 November 1993.
notes.explanation: The same date also splits the evacuation levels that the regulation's Table 1 requires.
notes.evidence: Certified refrigerant recovery or recycling equipment means equipment manufactured before November 15, 1993, that meets the standards in § 82.158(c), (e), or (g); equipment certified by an approved equipment testing organization to meet the standards in § 82.158(b), (d), or (f)
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.152 (eCFR), definition of “Certified refrigerant recovery or recycling equipment”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A shop still uses a recovery machine manufactured in 1991 that meets the standards set for equipment of that age. Does it count as certified recovery equipment?
notes.back: Yes. Equipment manufactured before 15 November 1993 that meets those standards counts as certified.
notes.explanation: For pre-1993 machines, meeting the standards is what makes them certified, without testing-organisation certification.
notes.evidence: Certified refrigerant recovery or recycling equipment means equipment manufactured before November 15, 1993, that meets the standards in § 82.158(c), (e), or (g); equipment certified by an approved equipment testing organization to meet the standards in § 82.158(b), (d), or (f)
notes.source: 40 CFR 82.152 (eCFR), definition of “Certified refrigerant recovery or recycling equipment”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Before used refrigerant can be resold to a new owner, who must reclaim it?
notes.back: An EPA-certified refrigerant reclaimer.
notes.explanation: The restriction covers used ozone-depleting and substitute refrigerants alike, HFCs included.
notes.evidence: restrict the resale of used ozone-depleting and substitute (e.g., HFC) refrigerant to a new owner unless it has been reclaimed by an EPA-certified refrigerant reclaimer.
notes.source: US EPA, Stationary Refrigeration Refrigerant Reclamation Requirements, “Refrigerant Reclamation Requirements”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Can recovered or recycled refrigerant go back into a system without being reclaimed?
notes.back: Yes, into the same system or other systems owned by the same person.
notes.explanation: Reclamation is needed when refrigerant passes to a new owner, not when it stays with the same one.
notes.evidence: Refrigerant that has been recovered and/or recycled can be returned to the same system or other systems owned by the same person without being reclaimed.
notes.source: US EPA, Stationary Refrigeration Refrigerant Reclamation Requirements, “Refrigerant Reclamation Requirements”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A technician recovers refrigerant from one customer's old unit and wants to sell it to a different customer. May they?
notes.back: No. Before used refrigerant can be sold it must be reclaimed by an EPA-certified reclaimer.
notes.explanation: The same answer notes that reclaimers and some distributors may pay for used refrigerant, which is the legal route to value.
notes.evidence: Before used refrigerant can be sold it must be reclaimed by an EPA certified reclaimer. Depending on the type of refrigerant and the level of contamination, EPA certified reclaimers and some distributors may offer money for it.
notes.source: US EPA, Questions and Answers for Section 608 Certified Technicians, “Can I sell used refrigerant that I recover from customers’ appliances?”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A contractor recovers refrigerant from one display case in a supermarket chain and charges it into another case the same chain owns. Must it be reclaimed first?
notes.back: No. It can go into other systems owned by the same person without being reclaimed.
notes.explanation: Ownership does not change, so the rule on resale to a new owner is not triggered.
notes.evidence: Refrigerant that has been recovered and/or recycled can be returned to the same system or other systems owned by the same person without being reclaimed.
notes.source: US EPA, Stationary Refrigeration Refrigerant Reclamation Requirements, “Refrigerant Reclamation Requirements”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Which transfers of used refrigerant between related companies are allowed without reclamation?
notes.back: Transfers between a parent company and its subsidiaries, or between subsidiaries with the same parent.
notes.explanation: It is one of the listed exceptions to the rule that used refrigerant sold on must be reclaimed.
notes.evidence: is being transferred between or among a parent company and one or more of its subsidiaries, or between or among subsidiaries having the same parent company;
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A reclaimer reprocesses recovered refrigerant but skips the laboratory analysis. Can the refrigerant be sold as properly reclaimed?
notes.back: No. Its purity must be verified using the laboratory protocol in AHRI Standard 700-2016.
notes.explanation: Reprocessing to the purity level is only half the rule; the verification by laboratory protocol is the other half.
notes.evidence: To be properly reclaimed, used refrigerant must be reprocessed to at least the purity level specified in Appendix A to 40 CFR Part 82, Subpart F [based on Air Conditioning, Heating, and Refrigeration Institute (AHRI) Standard 700-2016]. This purity level must be verified using the laboratory protocol set forth in this same standard.
notes.source: US EPA, Stationary Refrigeration Refrigerant Reclamation Requirements, “Refrigerant Reclamation Requirements”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Other than certified technicians, who can generally buy any type of ozone-depleting or substitute refrigerant?
notes.back: Employers of a Section 608 certified technician, or their authorised representatives, who give the wholesaler written evidence of that employment.
notes.explanation: The employer needs to show that it employs at least one properly certified technician.
notes.evidence: Employers of a Section 608 certified technician (or the employer's authorized representative) if the employer provides the refrigerant wholesaler with written evidence that he or she employs at least one properly certified technician.
notes.source: US EPA, Refrigerant Sales Restriction, “Requirements to Purchase Refrigerant”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Which containers does the sales restriction cover, and what does it not cover?
notes.back: Refrigerant in cylinders, cans or drums. Equipment or components already containing refrigerant are not covered.
notes.explanation: Small cans of substitute refrigerant for motor vehicle air conditioners are the carve-out within the containers.
notes.evidence: The sales restriction covers refrigerants contained in cylinders, cans, or drums, except for the sale of small cans of substitute refrigerants (e.g., R-134a for use in motor vehicle air conditioners). This sales restriction does not cover refrigeration and air-conditioning equipment or components containing refrigerants.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Since {{c1::1 January 2018}}, Section 608 certification has been required to buy HFCs for use in stationary refrigeration and air-conditioning systems.
notes.explanation: HFCs are not ozone-depleting, but they are potent greenhouse gases, and the restriction now covers them.
notes.evidence: Beginning January 1, 2018 EPA technician certification (EPA Section 608 certification) is required to purchase HFCs for use in stationary refrigeration and air-conditioning systems. While HFCs are not ozone-depleting substances, they are potent greenhouse gases that contribute to climate change.
notes.source: US EPA, Technicians and Contractors: Frequent Questions, “Are there any restrictions on the purchase of hydrofluorocarbon (HFC) refrigerants?”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A homeowner with no certification tries to buy a 25 lb cylinder of an HFC to top up their split system. May the wholesaler sell it?
notes.back: No. Since 1 January 2018 the sales restriction covers non-exempt substitutes such as HFCs.
notes.explanation: The buyer must be certified, employ a certified technician, or fall within another listed exception, and none applies here.
notes.evidence: No person may sell or distribute, or offer for sale or distribution, any substance that consists in whole or in part of a class I or class II substance or, starting on January 1, 2018, any non-exempt substitute for use as a refrigerant unless:
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A certified technician offers to use his card to buy refrigerant for an uncertified friend's own repair job. Is that allowed?
notes.back: No. Selling refrigerant for use in an appliance is a violation unless the recipient is, or employs, a certified technician.
notes.explanation: The rule looks at who will use the refrigerant, so a certified middleman does not make the sale lawful.
notes.evidence: It is a violation of EPA's regulations to sell, distribute, or offer for sale or distribution a refrigerant for use in an appliance, unless the recipient is, or employs, a certified technician.
notes.source: US EPA, Questions and Answers for Section 608 Certified Technicians, “Can I use my certification card to purchase refrigerant for a person that is not certified?”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Which MVAC refrigerant containers may still be sold without the buyer being certified?
notes.back: Containers of non-exempt substitute holding two pounds or less, with a unique fitting and, if made or imported from 2018, a self-sealing valve.
notes.explanation: All three conditions go together, and the refrigerant must be intended for use in an MVAC.
notes.evidence: The non-exempt substitute refrigerant is intended for use in an MVAC and is sold in a container designed to hold two pounds or less of refrigerant, has a unique fitting, and, if manufactured or imported on or after January 1, 2018, has a self-sealing valve that complies with the requirements of paragraph (c)(2) of this section.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: With the self-sealing valve closed, a small can of MVAC refrigerant may leak no more than {{c1::3.00 grams per year}}.
notes.explanation: The limit applies to partly used cans as well as new, full ones.
notes.evidence: The leakage rate from each container must not exceed 3.00 grams per year when the self-sealing valve is closed. This leakage rate applies to new, full containers as well as containers that may be partially full.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: An uncertified customer wants a small self-sealing can of HFC refrigerant to top up a window air conditioner at home. Does the small-can exception allow the sale?
notes.back: No. The exception covers only non-exempt substitute refrigerant intended for use in an MVAC.
notes.explanation: A window air conditioner is stationary equipment, so the MVAC small-can exception does not reach it.
notes.evidence: The non-exempt substitute refrigerant is intended for use in an MVAC and is sold in a container designed to hold two pounds or less of refrigerant, has a unique fitting, and, if manufactured or imported on or after January 1, 2018, has a self-sealing valve that complies with the requirements of paragraph (c)(2) of this section.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Can a Section 609 certified technician buy refrigerant intended for stationary equipment?
notes.back: No, regardless of container size.
notes.explanation: Only Section 608 certified technicians can buy refrigerant intended for stationary refrigeration and air-conditioning equipment.
notes.evidence: Only Section 608 certified technicians can purchase refrigerants intended for use with stationary refrigeration and air-conditioning equipment. Section 609 certified technicians cannot purchase refrigerants that are intended for use with stationary equipment, regardless of container size.
notes.source: US EPA, Refrigerant Sales Restriction, “Requirements to Purchase Refrigerant”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What must the invoices kept by sellers of class I, class II or non-exempt substitute refrigerant show?
notes.back: The purchaser's name, the date of sale and the quantity of refrigerant purchased.
notes.explanation: Non-exempt substitutes were added from 1 January 2018; sales of exempt substitutes and qualifying small MVAC cans are left out.
notes.evidence: Persons who sell or distribute, or offer to sell or distribute, any class I or class II refrigerant, or, starting on January 1, 2018, any non-exempt substitute refrigerant must keep invoices that indicate the name of the purchaser, the date of sale, and the quantity of refrigerant purchased
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What does the EPA recommend a wholesaler obtain from someone buying refrigerant for resale?
notes.back: A signed statement that they are buying it only for eventual resale to certified technicians.
notes.explanation: It is a recommendation, not a rule: the regulation does not specify the precautions wholesalers must take.
notes.evidence: Although the regulation does not specify precautions that wholesalers must take to verify the intent of individuals purchasing refrigerant, EPA recommends that wholesalers obtain a signed statement from the purchaser indicating that he or she is purchasing the refrigerant only for eventual resale to certified technicians.
notes.source: US EPA, Refrigerant Sales Restriction, “Wholesaler Responsibilities when Selling Refrigerant”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Which activities does the regulation list as reasonably expected to violate the integrity of the refrigerant circuit?
notes.back: Among others: attaching or detaching hoses and gauges, adding or removing refrigerant or components, and cutting the refrigerant line.
notes.explanation: The list is open (“include but are not limited to”), so other work can count too.
notes.evidence: Activities reasonably expected to violate the integrity of the refrigerant circuit include but are not limited to: Attaching or detaching hoses and gauges to and from the appliance; adding or removing refrigerant; adding or removing components; and cutting the refrigerant line.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: An electrician rewires the external electrical circuit of a rooftop unit and repaints its casing. Is that work reasonably expected to violate the refrigerant circuit?
notes.back: No. Painting and rewiring an external circuit are named as not reasonably expected to violate it.
notes.explanation: Replacing pipe insulation and tightening nuts and bolts are in the same list of activities that do not count.
notes.evidence: Activities such as painting the appliance, rewiring an external electrical circuit, replacing insulation on a length of pipe, or tightening nuts and bolts are not reasonably expected to violate the integrity of the refrigerant circuit.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: An installer connects the pre-charged lines of a new R-410A mini-split. Is Section 608 certification needed?
notes.back: Yes. Connecting or disconnecting hoses or pre-charged lines during installation requires Section 608 certification.
notes.explanation: Adding or removing refrigerant during installation needs it too; installation is not exempt.
notes.evidence: Adding or removing refrigerant from a mini-split as part of installation, and/or connecting or disconnecting hoses or pre-charged lines requires a section 608 technician certification.
notes.source: US EPA, Questions and Answers for Section 608 Certified Technicians, “Is technician certification required to install an R-410A mini-split?”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Apart from contractors' employees, who does the definition say could be technicians?
notes.back: Among others: installers, in-house service personnel, and owners or operators of appliances.
notes.explanation: The definition goes by what a person does, so owners doing their own circuit work are included.
notes.evidence: Technicians could include but are not limited to installers, contractor employees, in-house service personnel, and owners and/or operators of appliances.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Does the EPA require a separate “R-410A certification”?
notes.back: No. Section 608 certification goes by appliance type, whatever the refrigerant; R-410A-only courses are not equivalent to it.
notes.explanation: Some trade schools offered R-410A certificates because it differs from R-22 in operating pressure, among other things.
notes.evidence: EPA requires a section 608 certification regardless of refrigerant type based on the type of appliance (Type I, Type II, Type III, or Universal). However, EPA does not have a certification that is exclusively focused on R-410A.
notes.source: US EPA, Questions and Answers for Section 608 Certified Technicians, “Does EPA require an R-410A Certification?”

notes.front: A technician will service a commercial system charged with R-134a, a medium-pressure refrigerant. A summary says Type II covers only high- and very high-pressure appliances. Which certification applies?
notes.back: Type II. The regulation's Type II covers medium-, high- and very high-pressure appliances.
notes.explanation: The regulation text governs, and it names the medium-pressure class in Type II.
notes.evidence: Persons who maintain, service, repair, or dispose of medium-, high-, or very high-pressure appliances (except small appliances, MVACs, and MVAC-like appliances) must be certified as Type II technicians.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A technician is hired to repair a chiller charged with R-123. Which certification type does the job need?
notes.back: Type III, because R-123 is a low-pressure refrigerant.
notes.explanation: R-123 is one of the regulation's low-pressure examples, and low-pressure appliances fall under Type III.
notes.evidence: Low-pressure appliance means an appliance that uses a refrigerant with a liquid phase saturation pressure below 45 psia at 104 °F. Examples include but are not limited to appliances using R-11, R-123, R-113, and R-245fa.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A technician will repair the sealed refrigerant system of a window air conditioner. Which certification type covers it?
notes.back: Type I, because a window air conditioner is a small appliance.
notes.explanation: Room air conditioners, including window units, are named in the definition of small appliance.
notes.evidence: room air conditioners (including window air conditioners, portable air conditioners, and packaged terminal air heat pumps)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A technician's week spans household refrigerators, rooftop R-410A units and low-pressure chillers. Which single certification covers all of it?
notes.back: Universal certification.
notes.explanation: The work touches all three categories covered by Types I, II and III, which is what Universal is for.
notes.evidence: Persons who maintain, service, repair, or dispose of all appliances described in paragraph (a)(1)(i) through (iii) of this section must be certified as Universal technicians.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Is Section 608 certification required to dispose of small appliances, MVACs or MVAC-like appliances?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Disposing of any other appliance does require Section 608 certification.
notes.evidence: Section 608 technician certification is required to dispose of appliances, except for small appliances (an appliance that is fully manufactured, charged, and hermetically sealed in a factory with five pounds or less of refrigerant), motor vehicle air conditioners (MVACs), or MVAC-like appliances.
notes.source: US EPA, Questions and Answers for Section 608 Certified Technicians, “Is section 608 certification required to dispose of appliances?”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A scrapyard worker recovers refrigerant from old household refrigerators before crushing them. Does the worker need Section 608 certification?
notes.back: No. Persons who dispose of small appliances are not required to be certified.
notes.explanation: The refrigerant must still be properly recovered before disposal; only the certification requirement falls away.
notes.evidence: Persons who dispose of small appliances, MVACs, and MVAC-like appliances are not required to be certified.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A crew dismantles a rooftop R-410A unit for scrap. Does the person recovering its refrigerant need certification?
notes.back: Yes, Type II. Disposing of high-pressure appliances requires it.
notes.explanation: The no-certification rule for disposal covers only small appliances, MVACs and MVAC-like appliances.
notes.evidence: Persons who maintain, service, repair, or dispose of medium-, high-, or very high-pressure appliances (except small appliances, MVACs, and MVAC-like appliances) must be certified as Type II technicians.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: On what condition can an apprentice work on appliances before being certified?
notes.back: They must be closely and continuously supervised by a technician holding the right Section 608 certification for that type of appliance.
notes.explanation: The supervisor's certification has to match the appliance type being serviced, not just be any certificate.
