notes.evidence: Apprentices can work on appliances prior to certification if they are closely and continuously supervised by a technician that has the appropriate section 608 certification(s) for the type of appliance that is being serviced.
notes.source: US EPA, Questions and Answers for Section 608 Certified Technicians, “Can apprentices work on appliances prior to obtaining certification?”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A registered apprentice recovers refrigerant from a chiller while the certified technician is at another site across town. Is this allowed?
notes.back: No. The exemption requires the apprentice to be closely and continually supervised by a certified technician.
notes.explanation: Both the supervising technician and the apprentice are responsible for making sure the apprentice complies.
notes.evidence: closely and continually supervised by a certified technician while performing any maintenance, service, repair, or disposal that could reasonably be expected to release refrigerant from an appliance into the environment, except those substitute refrigerants exempted under paragraph (a)(1) of this section. The supervising certified technician and the apprentice have the responsibility to ensure that the apprentice complies with this subpart.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Someone first registered as an apprentice 30 months ago and still works uncertified under supervision. Are they still an apprentice?
notes.back: No. A person may be an apprentice only for two years from first registering.
notes.explanation: The exemption is a bridge to certification, time-limited from the date of first registration.
notes.evidence: A person may only be an apprentice for two years from the date of first registering with that office.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Where must a certified technician keep a copy of their certificate, and until when?
notes.back: At their place of business, until three years after they stop operating as a technician.
notes.explanation: The duty outlasts the career by three years, so retiring does not end it at once.
notes.evidence: Technicians certified under this section must keep a copy of their certificate at their place of business. (ii) Technicians must maintain a copy of their certificate until three years after no longer operating as a technician.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A technician retired in March 2024 and threw away his certificate copy in 2025. Was that allowed?
notes.back: No. He must keep a copy until three years after he stopped operating as a technician: March 2027.
notes.explanation: The three years run from leaving the trade, not from the date the certificate was issued.
notes.evidence: Technicians certified under this section must keep a copy of their certificate at their place of business. (ii) Technicians must maintain a copy of their certificate until three years after no longer operating as a technician.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Must a technician carry the certification card while servicing appliances?
notes.back: No, EPA does not require it, though customers may ask for proof of certification.
notes.explanation: EPA suggests keeping a picture of the certificate on your phone in case a customer asks.
notes.evidence: EPA does not require you to carry your certification card with you when servicing appliances, although some customers may inquire about whether you have proof of certification. You may want to consider keeping a picture of your certification on your phone in case asked by a customer.
notes.source: US EPA, Questions and Answers for Section 608 Certified Technicians, “Do I need to carry my certification card with me?”

notes.front: Do Section 608 technician certification credentials expire?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: A card earned years ago remains valid; the certificate does not need renewing on a cycle.
notes.evidence: Section 608 Technician Certification credentials do not expire.
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Requirements, “Requirements”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Can the EPA ever require technicians to recertify?
notes.back: It reserves the right to, if necessary, by placing a notice in the Federal Register.
notes.explanation: No such requirement is in force today, which is why current credentials do not expire.
notes.evidence: The Administrator reserves the right to specify a requirement for technician recertification at some future date, if necessary, by placing a notice in the Federal Register.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A technician certified in 1995 left the trade and now wants to return to refrigerant work. Must they retake the test?
notes.back: No. Section 608 credentials do not expire.
notes.explanation: Only a future recertification requirement, announced in the Federal Register, could change that.
notes.evidence: Section 608 Technician Certification credentials do not expire.
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Requirements, “Requirements”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What may the EPA require technicians to demonstrate at their place of business?
notes.back: Their ability to perform proper procedures for recovering and/or recycling refrigerant.
notes.explanation: Failing to demonstrate, or failing to use the equipment properly, may lead to the certificate being revoked or suspended.
notes.evidence: The Administrator may require technicians to demonstrate at their place of business their ability to perform proper procedures for recovering and/or recycling refrigerant, except those substitute refrigerants exempted under paragraph (a)(1) of this section. Failure to demonstrate or failure to properly use the equipment may result in revocation or suspension of the certificate.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: How many questions does each Type I, Type II or Type III test contain, and from which groups?
notes.back: 50: 25 from Group I (the core) and 25 from Group II (the sector-specific questions).
notes.explanation: Group II is sector-specific, so its 25 questions match the type being taken.
notes.evidence: All Type I, Type II and Type III, certification tests will include 25 questions from Group I and 25 questions from Group II.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82, Subpart F, Appendix D (eCFR), section d, “Test Content”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A Universal test has {{c1::100}} questions: 25 from Group I and 75 from Group II.
notes.explanation: The 75 technical questions are 25 from each of the three sector-specific areas.
notes.evidence: Universal certification tests will include 25 questions from Group I and 75 questions from Group II (with 25 from each of the three sector-specific areas).
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82, Subpart F, Appendix D (eCFR), section d, “Test Content”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: The passing score for the closed-book Type I, Type II, Type III and Universal tests is {{c1::70}} percent.
notes.explanation: Only the mail-in Type I test has a different pass mark.
notes.evidence: The passing score for the closed-book Type I, Type II, Type III and Universal certification test is 70 percent.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82, Subpart F, Appendix D (eCFR), section e, “Grading”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: The passing score for Type I tests taken in the mail-in format is {{c1::84}} percent.
notes.explanation: It is the one exception to the 70 percent pass mark that applies to the closed-book tests.
notes.evidence: The passing score for the closed-book Type I, Type II, Type III and Universal certification test is 70 percent. The passing score for Type I certification tests using the mail-in format is 84 percent.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82, Subpart F, Appendix D (eCFR), section e, “Grading”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Which certification tests must be closed-book and proctored in a secure environment?
notes.back: The Type II, Type III and Universal tests.
notes.explanation: For Universal, the condition applies whether it is taken as one test or as a series of tests.
notes.evidence: Technicians must pass a closed-book, proctored test, administered in a secure environment, by an EPA-approved certifying program to be certified as a Type II or Type III technician. Technicians must pass a closed-book, proctored test (or series of tests), administered in a secure environment, by an EPA-approved certifying program to be certified as a Universal technician.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82, Subpart F, Appendix D (eCFR), section a, “Test Preparation”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Can a Type I test taken in the mail-in format count towards Universal certification?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Universal needs every part passed closed-book and proctored in a secure environment, which a mail-in test is not.
notes.evidence: Technicians must pass a closed-book, proctored test (or series of tests), administered in a secure environment, by an EPA-approved certifying program to be certified as a Universal technician. Mail-in format Type I tests cannot be used toward a Universal certification.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82, Subpart F, Appendix D (eCFR), section a, “Test Preparation”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Can a core test taken as an open-book exam be used for Universal certification?
notes.back: No. The core test must be taken as a proctored exam to attain Universal certification.
notes.explanation: The same closed-book, proctored standard applies to the core as to the technical sections.
notes.evidence: Core tests taken as an open book exam cannot be used to get your Universal Certification. The core test must be taken as a proctored exam in order to attain Universal Certification.
notes.source: US EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Requirements, “Requirements”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A technician passed a proctored Type I test last year and proctored Type II and Type III tests this year. Can these be combined into Universal certification?
notes.back: Yes. Universal can be earned by combining passing scores on separate Type I, II and III tests.
notes.explanation: Universal need not be taken in one sitting, provided each part meets the closed-book, proctored conditions.
notes.evidence: Universal tests may be taken all at once, or by combining passing scores on separate Type I, Type II, and Type III tests.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82, Subpart F, Appendix D (eCFR), section a, “Test Preparation”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A technician passed a mail-in Type I test with 86 percent, then proctored Type II and Type III tests. Can they claim Universal certification?
notes.back: No. Mail-in Type I tests cannot be used towards Universal; they need a closed-book, proctored Type I test.
notes.explanation: The 86 percent clears the mail-in pass mark of 84, but the format, not the score, is what rules it out.
notes.evidence: Technicians must pass a closed-book, proctored test (or series of tests), administered in a secure environment, by an EPA-approved certifying program to be certified as a Universal technician. Mail-in format Type I tests cannot be used toward a Universal certification.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82, Subpart F, Appendix D (eCFR), section a, “Test Preparation”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A technician scores 68 percent on a proctored Type II test. Have they passed?
notes.back: No. The passing score for the closed-book tests is 70 percent.
notes.explanation: Type II is always closed-book, so the 70 percent pass mark applies.
notes.evidence: The passing score for the closed-book Type I, Type II, Type III and Universal certification test is 70 percent.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82, Subpart F, Appendix D (eCFR), section e, “Grading”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A technician scores 80 percent on a mail-in Type I test. Have they passed?
notes.back: No. The mail-in Type I pass mark is 84 percent.
notes.explanation: 80 percent would pass a closed-book test, but the mail-in format has its own, higher pass mark.
notes.evidence: The passing score for Type I certification tests using the mail-in format is 84 percent.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82, Subpart F, Appendix D (eCFR), section e, “Grading”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: How soon after an in-person test must a certifying programme issue the wallet-sized card?
notes.back: No later than 30 days from the date of the test.
notes.explanation: For mail-in Type I tests, the 30 days run from when the programme receives the completed test and documents.
notes.evidence: Certifying programs must issue a standard wallet-sized identification card no later than 30 days from the date of the test. Type I certifying programs using mail-in formats must issue cards to certified technicians no later than 30 days from the date the certifying program receives the completed test and any required documentation.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82, Subpart F, Appendix D (eCFR), section f, “Proof of Certification”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: How can a candidate arrange to take the certification test orally?
notes.back: By asking the programme in writing, with the reason, at least 30 days before the scheduled exam date.
notes.explanation: The request goes to the certifying programme, not to the EPA, and must explain why it is made.
notes.evidence: A test may be administered orally to any person who makes this request, in writing, to the program at least 30 days before the scheduled date for the examination. The written request must explain why the request is being made.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A technician has lost their certification card. Whom should they contact for a replacement?
notes.back: The company that certified them, whose name is on the certification card.
notes.explanation: The EPA itself does not issue certification cards; the certifying organisation does.
notes.evidence: Contact the company that certified you. The company's name is on the certification card.
notes.source: US EPA, Questions and Answers for Section 608 Certified Technicians, “How do I get a replacement certification card?”

notes.front: Under Subpart F, do the leak repair requirements of 82.157 apply to appliances containing only substitute refrigerants, such as HFCs?
notes.back: No. Since 10 April 2020, 82.157 covers only appliances holding 50 lb or more of class I or II refrigerant, or a blend containing one.
notes.explanation: The 2020 rule removed the substitute leak repair duties added in 2016. Separately, since 1 January 2026, a rule outside Subpart F (section 84.106) requires leak repair in many HFC appliances of 15 lb or more.
notes.evidence: As of April 10, 2020, this section applies only to appliances with a full charge of 50 or more pounds of any class I or class II refrigerant or blend containing a class I or class II refrigerant.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A 300 lb HFC system leaks heavily. The owner reasons that, as Subpart F’s leak repair section does not cover HFCs, no Section 608 rule applies. Is that right?
notes.back: No. Certification, the sales restriction, safe disposal, evacuation, reclamation and certified recovery equipment still apply to HFCs.
notes.explanation: Only the leak repair provisions were rescinded for substitutes in 2020. And since 1 January 2026 a separate rule outside Subpart F (section 84.106) requires leak repair in many HFC appliances of 15 lb or more.
notes.evidence: This action does not rescind the applicability of the other provisions that were extended to certain substitute refrigerants (e.g., HFCs) such as the sales restriction and technician certification requirement, safe disposal requirements, evacuation requirements, reclamation standards, and requirement to use certified recovery equipment.
notes.source: US EPA, Regulatory Updates: Section 608 Refrigerant Management Regulations, “Recent Regulatory Developments”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What must the final processor of a small appliance, MVAC or MVAC-like appliance do about its refrigerant?
notes.back: Either recover any remaining refrigerant, or verify with a signed statement or contract that it has already been recovered.
notes.explanation: Refrigerant that had already leaked out is set apart; the duty concerns refrigerant that had not leaked previously.
notes.evidence: Recover any remaining refrigerant from the appliance in accordance with paragraph (a) of this section; or (2) Verify using a signed statement or a contract that all refrigerant that had not leaked previously has been recovered
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What must a signed statement given to a final processor include?
notes.back: The name and address of the person who recovered the refrigerant, and the date it was recovered.
notes.explanation: Those details make the statement traceable to a named recoverer and a date.
notes.evidence: If using a signed statement, it must include the name and address of the person who recovered the refrigerant and the date the refrigerant was recovered.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A scrap dealer receives a load of old refrigerators with a signed note, “refrigerant removed”, that gives no date or address for whoever removed it. Is that an adequate signed statement?
notes.back: No. It must include the recoverer's name and address and the date the refrigerant was recovered.
notes.explanation: Without those details the dealer, as final processor, has not verified recovery and must recover the refrigerant itself.
notes.evidence: If using a signed statement, it must include the name and address of the person who recovered the refrigerant and the date the refrigerant was recovered.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: If all the refrigerant has leaked out of an appliance before delivery, what must the final processor obtain?
notes.back: A signed statement that all the refrigerant leaked out before delivery and that recovery is not possible.
notes.explanation: Without such a statement, the final processor is back to recovering or verifying recovery.
notes.evidence: If all the refrigerant has leaked out of the appliance, the final processor must obtain a signed statement that all the refrigerant in the appliance had leaked out prior to delivery to the final processor and recovery is not possible.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A supplier cut the lines of some freezers to let the refrigerant out, then signed that the refrigerant “leaked out”. Does that count as leaked out?
notes.back: No. Leaked out excludes releases caused by negligence or deliberate acts such as cutting refrigerant lines.
notes.explanation: Only system failures, accidents or other unavoidable occurrences count as leaking out.
notes.evidence: in this context means those situations in which the refrigerant has escaped because of system failures, accidents, or other unavoidable occurrences not caused by a person's negligence or deliberate acts such as cutting refrigerant lines.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A final processor must keep copies of the signed statements or contracts on site for {{c1::three years}}.
notes.explanation: Hard copy or electronic format are both acceptable.
notes.evidence: must keep a copy of all the signed statements or contracts obtained under paragraph (b)(2) of this section on site, in hard copy or in electronic format, for three years.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.back: Those evacuating appliances with a full charge of more than 5 and less than 50 pounds for disposal; for three years.
notes.explanation: The duty has applied since 1 January 2018 and falls on the technician doing the evacuation.

notes.front: A technician recovers refrigerant from a 12 lb residential split system before it is scrapped. What must be recorded for that appliance?
notes.back: The company name, the appliance's location, the date of recovery and the type of refrigerant recovered.
notes.explanation: A 12 lb system falls in the more-than-5, less-than-50 pound band, so the disposal records rule applies.
notes.evidence: The company name, location of the appliance, date of recovery, and type of refrigerant recovered for each appliance;

notes.front: What must a small appliance be equipped with before it can be sold?
notes.back: A process stub, to make removal of refrigerant at servicing and disposal easier.
notes.explanation: Other appliances need a servicing aperture for the same purpose; appliances using only exempt substitutes are excepted.
notes.evidence: unless it is equipped with a process stub to facilitate the removal of refrigerant at servicing and disposal.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: What must an appliance other than a small appliance have before it can be sold?
notes.back: A servicing aperture, to make removal of refrigerant at servicing and disposal easier.
notes.explanation: Appliances containing only exempted refrigerants are left out of this requirement.
notes.evidence: unless it is equipped with a servicing aperture to facilitate the removal of refrigerant at servicing and disposal.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A supplier offers “R-22a” as a replacement for R-22 in an existing air conditioner. Is it approved for that use?
notes.back: No. Refrigerants with 22a in their names are highly flammable, propane-based and not approved for existing air-conditioning systems.
notes.explanation: They have never been submitted to the EPA for review of their health and environmental impacts.
notes.evidence: are highly flammable substances that are not approved for use in existing air-conditioning systems. These refrigerants have never been submitted to EPA for review of their health and environmental impacts. Using these propane-based refrigerants
notes.source: US EPA, Resources for Stationary Refrigeration and Air-Conditioning Equipment Technicians, “Flammable Refrigerants and Technician Safety”
